inicio.text:
Astra is a generic and modular tabletop RPG system, designed to serve as a base for different settings, genres and play styles.
Its structure takes as its main reference the systems of the Storyteller family, especially their most recent editions, using dice pools and an approach centered on characters, conflicts and consequences. At the same time, it brings in concepts inspired by systems such as Savage Worlds Adventure Edition (SWADE), Pathfinder and Dungeons & Dragons, mainly in aspects related to modularity, character customization and tactical combat.
Astra was conceived with a philosophy similar to that of an open source software project: there is a consistent rules core, on top of which different modules, adaptations and settings can be built without all of them having to use exactly the same tools.
The system is tightly integrated with Foundry Virtual Tabletop, which works as its main digital implementation. The goal, however, is not to limit Astra to the virtual table: its rules are designed so they can be used both at in-person tables and on other platforms.
Start here
To get to know the system, this is the recommended reading order:
Basic Mechanics — understand how tests are built and resolved.
Characters — learn the characters' capabilities and resources.
Character Creation — build a complete character.
Scenes and Conflicts — see how scenes, turns and confrontations work.
System rules
The core is organized into nine main areas:
Basic Mechanics — resolving tests and results.
Characters — the characters' capabilities, resources, motivations and traits.
Competencies — sets of Capabilities that change what the character can do.
Creatures — creature types and traits specific to NPCs.
Scenes and Conflicts — structure of tactical scenes, turns and confrontation actions.
Moving — getting around and actions related to movement.
Equipment — load, common items, weapons, armor, shields and switching items.
Resistance and Vulnerability — how characters and creatures react to damage types.
Conditions — states that affect characters during a scene.
Character creation
Character creation overview
Identity — Concept, Ambition, Desire and Convictions.
Attributes and Skills — fixed Attribute array and Skill profiles.
Derived Traits — Health, Willpower, Initiative and Maximum Load.
Competencies — 2 Competency Points.
Starting Equipment — starting equipment defined by the setting.

regras/mecanica-basica/reserva-de-dados.summary: The Dice Pool is the number of dice used to resolve an action whose outcome is uncertain. When a character tries to do something that requires a test, the rule in use or the Narrator determines which Skill applies. The…
regras/mecanica-basica/reserva-de-dados.text:
The Dice Pool is the number of dice used to resolve an action whose outcome is uncertain.
When a character tries to do something that requires a test, the rule in use or the Narrator determines which Skill applies. The Skill brings its linked Attribute, unless a rule sets a replacement. When no Skill applies, the rule or the Narrator names only the Attribute. The values of these traits are added together to form the test's Dice Pool.
The larger the Dice Pool, the better the character's chances of a good result.
Dice Used
Astra uses ten-sided dice, written with the abbreviation d10.
Each point that makes up a Dice Pool is one d10 to be rolled.
For example, a Dice Pool of 5 dice means the player must roll:
5d10
The results on those dice are then read individually to determine how many Successes were achieved.
Building a Dice Pool
In most tests, a Dice Pool is formed by combining a Skill with its linked Attribute.
Attribute + Skill = Dice Pool
For example, a character trying to slip quietly through a guarded area might use:
Agility + Stealth
If the character has Agility 3 and Stealth 2, their Dice Pool is 5 dice.
The player then rolls those five dice at the same time.
The action taken determines which Skill applies. Each Skill has a linked Attribute, listed in Skills, and uses that Attribute unless a rule sets a replacement.
When no Skill applies to the action, the Dice Pool is formed by the Attribute alone. For example, resisting a poison might use only Vigor.
Every Dice Pool has at least one Attribute. The second part, when there is one, is a Skill or another Attribute — never the same Attribute twice.
Determining the Attribute
When a Pool uses a Skill, determine its Attribute in this order:
the Skill sets its linked Attribute;
an Action, equipment or another rule can replace that Attribute;
a Capability can set another Attribute and always takes precedence over the previous steps.
For example, Fighting is linked to Agility. A melee Attack normally uses Agility + Fighting. If the weapon has a property that sets Strength, the Attack uses Strength + Fighting. If a Capability sets Cunning as the Attribute of that Attack, the final Pool is Cunning + Fighting.
Only the final Attribute is added to the Skill. The replaced and replacing Attributes are never added together.
Penalties
Dice penalties, such as those from Prone, Debilitated, Grappled and Overload, add up. A character who is Prone and Debilitated, for example, suffers -4 dice.
The Physical or Spiritual category of a roll is determined by the Attribute actually used, including after a replacement. When the Pool combines two Attributes of different categories, the penalties of both categories apply, and they also add up.
If penalties reduce the Dice Pool to less than 1 die, the character does not roll, and their result counts as 1 Success, just like a target without a response.
Making the Test
After determining the Dice Pool, roll all the dice in it.
Each die that reaches the value needed to count as a Success adds one Success to the test's result.
The total number of Successes determines the outcome of the action.
In simple tests, a certain number of Successes may be enough to perform the action. In opposed situations, the Successes of two characters can be compared directly.
Example
A character has:
Agility 3
Stealth 2
To slip past a guard unnoticed, the Narrator asks for an Agility + Stealth test.
The character's Dice Pool is:
3 + 2 = 5 dice
The player rolls five dice and counts the Successes.
The result of that roll determines whether the character gets through the area without being noticed.
Successes and Failures
When making a test, each die of the Dice Pool is read individually.
A die showing 6 or more is a Success.
Result Effect 
1 - 5 Failure 
6 - 9 1 Success 
10 1 Success (a pair of 10s grants 1 extra Success) 
A result of 1 has no special effect: it simply does not count as a Success.
After rolling all the dice, add up the total number of Successes.
The roll succeeds when the number of Successes is equal to or greater than the test's Difficulty.
If the character does not reach the required number of Successes, the test is a Failure.
Difficulty Scale
A test's Difficulty sets how many Successes are needed for the action to succeed. The table below is only a suggested calibration, not a firm rule — the Narrator can adjust it to the situation.
Difficulty Description 
1 Routine — almost always works 
2 Basic — standard for most tests 
3 Challenging — takes a little effort 
4 Hard — needs a good Pool 
5 Very hard — few even try 
6+ Feat — reserved for extraordinary deeds 
An average character (Attribute 2 + Skill 2, a Pool of 4 dice) has good odds at Difficulty 2. Use it as a starting point.
Extra Successes
Matching the Difficulty already guarantees success. Each Success above the Difficulty, however, deserves special treatment: the action can be finished faster, more elegantly or more discreetly, reveal extra information, or open new opportunities. The bigger the surplus, the more impressive the result — it is up to the Narrator to reward the surplus narratively.
Pairs of 10s
Results of 10 have a special property.
When two dice show 10 on the same roll, they form a pair of 10s. Each pair grants 1 extra Success, on top of the 2 Successes the dice already produced.
10 + 10 = 3 Successes
Each pair of 10s is counted separately. An unpaired 10 still counts normally as 1 Success.
For example, the results:
10, 10, 10, 7, 3
produce 5 Successes: the pair of 10s produces 3 Successes (2 + 1 extra), the third 10 produces 1 Success and the 7 produces 1 more Success.
Success Counting Example
A character makes a test with a Dice Pool of 5 dice and gets:
2, 6, 10, 10, 4
The 6 produces 1 Success, while the pair of 10s produces 3 Successes (2 + 1 extra), for a total of 4 Successes.
If the test's Difficulty is 4 or less, the action succeeds.
If the Difficulty is 5 or more, the action is a Failure.
Attribute Replacements
A Skill only uses another Attribute when an Action, equipment, Capability or other rule expressly says so. Describing the same action in a different way does not, by itself, change the linked Attribute.
A replacement follows these principles:
it swaps one Attribute for another, without adding both;
its effect is limited to the Skill, Action, Pool or formula it names;
replacements do not chain to add several Attributes;
when more than one optional replacement is available, the character picks only one;
a Capability always takes precedence over a replacement set by an Action, equipment or other earlier rule.
For example, Persuasion is linked to Charisma. A Capability can let the character use Cunning + Persuasion without changing their other Charisma or Cunning tests.
The narrative approach can still change the applicable Skill, the Difficulty, the effects of a win or failure and any circumstantial bonuses or penalties. It just does not freely replace a Skill's Attribute.
Help
Other characters can help whoever is making a test, provided they are adjacent to them. Helpers do not roll dice. Help adds +1 die to the Dice Pool of whoever makes the test.
There is no limit on helpers, but the bonus does not stack: the test gets at most +1 die of help, no matter how many characters help.
In a Tactical Scene, helping uses the helper's Action.
Example: a character with Research 2 looks for information in a library with two allies helping. Their Pool gets +1 die.

regras/personagens/atributos.text:
Attributes represent a character's fundamental abilities. They describe their physical and spiritual aptitudes and are part of most Dice Pools used during play.
Whenever an action calls for a test, a Skill is usually combined with its linked Attribute to form the Dice Pool.
For example, lifting a heavy object might call for Strength, while quickly noticing something out of the ordinary might involve Cunning.
Categories
Each Attribute belongs to a category: Physical or Spiritual.
Category Attributes 
Physical Strength, Agility, Vigor 
Spiritual Charisma, Determination, Cunning 
Some rules affect only rolls of one category, such as the penalties of Debilitated, Overload and full Willpower. In those cases, the category of the Attribute actually used in the Dice Pool applies. If a rule replaces the Attribute, the replacement's category applies instead. If the Pool uses two Attributes of different categories, the penalties of both categories apply.
Linked Attributes and replacements
Each Skill has a linked Attribute, which forms its default Pool. The narrative description of the action does not allow freely swapping that Attribute.
Actions, equipment, Capabilities and other rules can set express replacements. A replacement swaps one Attribute for another without adding the two values together. When a Capability sets a Pool's Attribute, it always takes precedence over Actions, equipment and earlier rules.
Capabilities can also replace Attributes in fixed formulas, such as Health, Willpower, Load or Initiative. That replacement affects only the given formula and does not change the other roles of the Attributes involved.
List of Attributes
Strength
Represents the character's physical power.
It is used to lift, carry, push, break or exert force against something. It is linked to Athletics and Throwing, takes part in physical Maneuvers, sets Load and replaces Agility on Attacks made with Heavy weapons.
Agility
Represents coordination, reflexes and bodily precision.
It is used in actions that depend on quick movements, balance, motor control or physical precision. It is the default Attribute for melee and shooting-weapon Attacks, and is linked to Acrobatics, Shooting, Riding, Driving, Stealth, Fighting, Piloting and Sleight of Hand.
Vigor
Represents physical endurance, toughness and the ability to withstand effort.
It is used to resist fatigue, harsh conditions and other situations that put the body to the test. It also sets the default number of boxes on the Health track.
Charisma
Represents presence, personal magnetism and the ability to influence other people.
It is used when the character tries to inspire, please, impress, persuade, deceive or lead someone in a given direction. It is linked to Animal Empathy, Intimidation, Deception, Performance and Persuasion.
Determination
Represents focus, discipline, emotional stability and mental strength.
It is used to keep concentration, stay calm, persist in the face of hardship and resist provocations, pressures and influences that try to steer the character away from their goals. It also sets the default number of boxes on the Willpower track and, together with Cunning, forms the Initiative Pool.
Cunning
Represents knowledge, reasoning, quick thinking and perception.
It is used to understand problems, research, remember information, notice the surroundings, improvise and find solutions — including under time pressure. It is linked to General Knowledge, Repair, Healing, Scholarship, Navigation, Occultism, Perception, Research and Survival. It also takes part in Initiative and limits the normal stacks of Aiming.

regras/personagens/pericias.text:
Skills represent trained abilities and areas of expertise a character has developed through practice, study or experience. They do not describe innate talent, but what the character has learned to do.
Each Skill has a linked Attribute, normally used to form its Dice Pool.
Linked Attribute + Skill = Dice Pool
The description of the action sets which Skill applies, but does not freely swap its Attribute. Actions, equipment, Capabilities and other rules can set express replacements.
List of Skills
Skill Linked Attribute Description 
Acrobatics Agility Dodging, keeping balance, breaking falls and performing precise body movements. 
Throwing Strength Hurling weapons and objects directly with the body, such as knives, spears, stones and grenades. 
Shooting Agility Firing projectile weapons, such as bows, crossbows and firearms. 
Athletics Strength Running, jumping, climbing, swimming and other feats of physical power. 
Riding Agility Mounting, steering and keeping control of ridden animals. 
General Knowledge Cunning Common knowledge of the world and of one's own culture: customs, places, laws, figures and news. 
Repair Cunning Repairing, assembling and taking apart mechanisms, equipment and structures. 
Healing Cunning Treating wounds, illnesses and other physical conditions. 
Driving Agility Driving motorized land vehicles. 
Animal Empathy Charisma Calming, training, understanding and bonding with animals. 
Scholarship Cunning Academic knowledge: history, sciences, literate culture and the like. 
Stealth Agility Moving unnoticed, hiding and acting silently.

regras/personagens/tamanho.text:
Size gives the physical build of a character or creature and how much space they take up on the map during a Tactical Scene.
Every character has a Size. The default is Medium.
Size Space taken up 
Tiny ½ × ½ square 
Small 1 × 1 square 
Medium 1 × 1 square 
Large 2 × 2 squares 
Huge 3 × 3 squares 
Colossal 4 × 4 squares 
A creature that takes up more than one square is considered adjacent to everything next to any of the squares it occupies, including diagonally.
Moving another creature
A creature can only move another creature of the same Size or smaller.
This applies to every rule that moves a character against their will, such as the Reposition Maneuver or dragging a Grappled target. A smaller creature can still try to Trip, Grapple or Disarm a larger one, but cannot move it from its place.
Size in the Attack
Attacking a much larger target is easier, and attacking a much smaller target is harder. Count the difference in categories between the attacker and the target:
Target Attack 
2 categories larger +2 dice 
3 or more categories larger +4 dice 
2 or more categories smaller -2 dice 
One category of difference changes nothing. The rule works both ways: a cat attacking a dragon gets +4 dice, and the dragon attacking the cat gets -2.
Settings and modules can define additional rules for Size.

regras/personagens/vida.text:
Health represents a character's physical condition and their ability to keep acting after being wounded.
Whenever a character takes damage, that damage is recorded on their Health track. As wounds pile up, their condition worsens until they can no longer carry on as usual.
Health does not represent only visible wounds. It can also represent physical exhaustion, trauma, burns, bruises and other consequences that can compromise the character's body.
Health Track
Each character has a limited number of boxes on their Health track.
When they take damage, the player marks a number of boxes equal to the damage taken.
Boxes are filled from left to right.
A character's Health track has:
3 + Vigor boxes
Vigor is the Health Attribute by default. Settings, Capabilities and other rules can adjust this value or replace the Attribute used in the formula.
When a Capability replaces Vigor, the number of boxes is immediately recalculated from the new Attribute. The replacement affects only the size of the track: recovery, Vigor tests and other rules are not changed, unless the Capability itself says otherwise.
Damage Severity
Astra uses two main damage severities:
Superficial Damage
Aggravated Damage
The difference between them represents how serious the wound is and how hard it is to recover from.
The Damage Type — the nature of the wound (slashing, bludgeoning, piercing, fire, ice, electric etc.) — is separate from severity: it is set by the damage source, such as weapons (see Weapons).
Superficial Damage
Superficial Damage represents less serious wounds, physical wear and trauma that a character can recover from with relative ease.
Unarmed blows, light impacts and other wounds that do not put the character's physical integrity at immediate risk are examples of superficial damage, when the damage source or the Narrator says so. Aggravated wounds can also become superficial through armor, Resistances and other effects.
Superficial damage is recorded on the Health track as a / mark.
Aggravated Damage
Aggravated Damage represents serious and potentially incapacitating wounds.
Deep punctures, severe burns, lethal electricity and other especially dangerous forms of damage can deal aggravated damage.
This damage severity represents more serious consequences and is usually harder to recover from than superficial damage.
Certain equipment, Capabilities or effects can turn aggravated damage into superficial damage.
By default, all damage is aggravated — unless the damage source itself (weapon, Attack, effect) says otherwise. This is the case for most Attacks, especially those made with weapons. Armor and Resistances can convert aggravated damage to superficial (see Resistance and Vulnerability).
The main exception is unarmed combat, which deals superficial damage by default — punches, kicks and grabs are rarely fatal. The Narrator can also decide that other damage sources deal superficial damage when the situation calls for it.
Aggravated damage is recorded on the Health track as an X mark.
Full Health Track
When the Health track is full, with any mix of superficial and aggravated damage, the character becomes Debilitated (see Debilitated).
If they keep taking damage, superficial or aggravated, and there are no free boxes left, the extra damage starts converting boxes already filled with superficial damage into aggravated damage.
When the whole Health track is filled with aggravated damage, the character is incapacitated and in a potentially fatal situation. In practical terms, they can no longer carry on normally in the scene, and survival depends on the situation and the Narrator's narrative decision.
Recovery
Wounds do not disappear as soon as a conflict ends.
Recovery depends on the severity of the damage taken.
Superficial Damage — heals with time, with no need for treatment. On completing a Long Rest, the character recovers an amount of superficial damage equal to their Vigor.
Aggravated Damage — does not recover with time. It stays on the track until it receives treatment, which converts it to superficial damage; the converted damage then heals normally.
Treatment is a care scene that requires minimum conditions: Healing supplies, hygiene and some comfort. Whoever treats rolls Cunning + Healing (the character themselves or someone else). Each success converts 1 point of aggravated damage to superficial. With no successes, the treatment converts nothing. A character can receive one treatment per in-game day.
If the character is hospitalized, in proper facilities, no roll is needed: they convert 1 point of aggravated damage to superficial per in-game day, until fully recovered.

regras/personagens/vontade.text:
Willpower represents a character's determination, focus and ability to keep acting under pressure.
While Health represents the character's physical condition, Willpower represents their mental and emotional endurance in difficult situations.
It can be used to withstand fear, pressure, suffering, psychological influence or other circumstances that can shake the character's resolve.
Willpower Track
Each character has a limited number of boxes on their Willpower track.
The track represents how much mental and emotional strain the character can bear before their ability to act is compromised.
When the character takes Willpower damage, that damage is recorded on the track the same way as damage on the Health track.
Boxes are filled from left to right.
A character's Willpower track has:
3 + Determination boxes
Determination is the Willpower Attribute by default. Settings, Capabilities and other rules can adjust this value or replace the Attribute used in the formula.
When a Capability replaces Determination, the number of boxes is immediately recalculated from the new Attribute. The replacement affects only the size of the track: Determination tests, Initiative and other rules are not changed, unless the Capability itself says otherwise.
Willpower Damage
Like Health, Willpower can take both damage severities:
Superficial Damage
Aggravated Damage
The difference between them represents how severe the psychological impact on the character is.
Unlike physical damage, Willpower damage has no default severity: it is always set by the source that causes it — for example, using Willpower to Reroll Dice deals superficial damage.
Superficial Damage
Superficial Willpower damage represents stress, anxiety, frustration, momentary fear, emotional pressure and other strain that the character can recover from relatively quickly.
This damage severity usually represents hard situations that leave no deep psychological consequences.
Aggravated Damage
Aggravated Willpower damage represents serious psychological trauma or situations that can deeply affect the character's state of mind.
Especially violent, terrifying or supernatural experiences can deal aggravated Willpower damage.
This damage severity is harder to recover from and can stay with the character for long periods.
Each Fracture a Conviction receives deals 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage (see Convictions and Pillars).
Full Willpower
As the Willpower track fills with superficial damage, the character nears their emotional and mental limit. When there are no boxes left, the character is under heavy psychological strain and suffers a -2 dice penalty on every roll that uses a Spiritual Attribute.
If they keep taking damage, superficial or aggravated, and there are no free boxes left, the extra damage converts boxes already filled with superficial damage into aggravated damage, as on the Health track.
If the whole track is filled with aggravated damage, the character may become unable to keep reacting normally to the situation. The -2 dice penalty then applies to every roll, of any category, and they suffer consequences that depend on the origin and nature of the trauma.
This does not necessarily mean unconsciousness or total loss of control. The consequence can take different forms, such as:
freezing in the face of the situation;
emotional collapse;
flight;
giving up;
momentary loss of control;
inability to keep facing a given threat.
The specific consequence depends on the circumstances of the scene and the Narrator's decisions for that situation.
Using Willpower
Willpower can be used to let a character briefly push past their own limits.
When using Willpower, the character takes 1 point of superficial Willpower damage and chooses one of the effects below.
A character with a full Willpower track cannot use Willpower, except to Break Limit.
Once per session, in total, a Conviction lets them use Willpower without taking the superficial damage, even with a full track (see Convictions and Pillars).
Some Capabilities granted by Competencies require using Willpower to be activated.
Reroll Dice
After making a test, the character can take 1 point of superficial Willpower damage to reroll up to 3 dice of their Dice Pool.
The player chooses which dice are rerolled and must use the new results.
It is possible to reroll more than once on the same test, taking 1 point of superficial Willpower damage each time.
On an opposed roll, whoever started the action (for example, the attacker in a Confront) decides first whether to reroll. Then the other participant decides.
This lets the character insist on an important action, even when the first attempt did not produce the desired result.
Ignore Physical Penalties
The character can also take 1 point of superficial Willpower damage to ignore, on the roll where Willpower is used, the dice penalties caused by their physical condition, such as those of Debilitated, Prone, Grappled and Overload.
This includes penalties caused by filling their Health track.
For example, a Debilitated character normally suffers -2 dice on rolls that use a Physical Attribute. By using Willpower, they can ignore that penalty on that roll.
This use represents the character forcing their own body to keep working despite the pain, exhaustion or severity of their wounds.
The superficial Willpower damage taken to use these effects is marked on the Willpower track as usual.
Break Limit
When the Willpower track is full and still has superficial damage on it, the character can keep Rerolling Dice by Breaking Limit.
Each use of Break Limit converts 1 point of superficial Willpower damage into aggravated damage, instead of the usual superficial damage.

A Long Rest represents several continuous hours of rest, usually a night's sleep, in conditions that let the character rest and recover.
On completing a Long Rest, the character:

headings.title: Ambition and Desire in the Story

regras/personagens/ambicao-e-desejo.text:
Characters are defined not only by their abilities, but also by what they want to achieve.
Ambition and Desire represent the goals that guide a character's decisions during the story. Both show what they are after, but they work on different scales.
Ambition represents a long-term goal, while Desire represents something the character means to achieve more immediately.
Each character has 1 Ambition and 1 Desire at a time.
These elements help set clear motivations for the character and give the Narrator tools to create conflicts, opportunities and consequences tied to the players' interests.
Ambition
Ambition represents an important, lasting goal for the character.
Usually, an Ambition cannot be completed in a single scene or session. It can take several steps, decisions or events before it is reached.
An Ambition can be about power, knowledge, revenge, recognition, protection, wealth, discovery or any other goal that matters to the character.
Examples of Ambitions include:
winning a position of influence;
finding a missing person;

regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.title: Convictions and Pillars
regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.summary: A Conviction is a principle the character refuses to betray — for example, "Never abandon those who fight at my side". Unlike Ambition and Desire, a Conviction is not a goal: it is a line of conduct.
regras/personagens/conviccoes-e-pilares.text:
A Conviction is a principle the character refuses to betray — for example, "Never abandon those who fight at my side".
Unlike Ambition and Desire, a Conviction is not a goal: it is a line of conduct.
Convictions
Every character has 3 Convictions, chosen during character creation (see Identity).
Pillars
Each Conviction must be sustained by a Pillar: a concrete person, place or object in the story that embodies that Conviction — for example, a traveling companion or a father's diary.
The Pillar gives the Narrator something tangible to put at risk.
Fractures
Each Conviction withstands 2 Fractures. A Conviction can be:
Intact — no Fractures;
with 1 Fracture;
with 2 Fractures, which breaks it (see Broken Conviction).
Gaining a Fracture
A Conviction gains 1 Fracture when:
the character deliberately acts against it; or
its Pillar is harmed or corrupted.
On gaining a Fracture, the character takes 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage.
Repairing a Fracture
At the end of a session in which the character defended a Conviction that is not broken, or its Pillar, paying a real cost — such as risk, loss or sacrifice —, remove 1 Fracture from that Conviction. Repairing a Fracture turns 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage into superficial damage.
This can happen once per session for each Conviction.
Broken Conviction
A Conviction breaks when:
it receives its second Fracture; or
its Pillar is destroyed or lost. In that case, the Conviction goes straight to 2 Fractures, and the character takes 1 point of aggravated Willpower damage for each Fracture gained this way.
While there are broken Convictions, every purchase made with XP costs 2 more XP for each broken Conviction, up to a maximum of 6 more XP.
Restoring a Broken Conviction
A broken Conviction is not repaired through Fractures. During the campaign, the character must actively seek that restoration in the story.
The player and the Narrator decide together whether the Conviction will be restored or replaced by a new Conviction, with its own Pillar.
Restored — including when the lost Pillar is recovered: the Conviction loses both Fractures, gets its Pillar back and up to 2 points of aggravated Willpower damage become superficial.
Replaced — the new Conviction starts intact, with no Fractures.
Benefit
Once per session, in total and not for each Conviction, when the character acts in defense of a Conviction or its Pillar, they can use Willpower without taking the superficial Willpower damage, whether to Reroll Dice or to Ignore Physical Penalties.
This use is possible even with a full Willpower track.
A broken Conviction does not grant this benefit.
Convictions in the Story
The Narrator can use Pillars to create dilemmas between the character's Convictions, their Ambition and their Desire — for example, when protecting a Pillar means giving up progress toward the Ambition.
Convictions do not dictate how the character must act. The player always decides what to do; the Fractures record the consequences of that choice.

regras/personagens/progressao.title: Advancement
regras/personagens/progressao.summary: In Astra, characters have no global levels. They grow gradually by acquiring and improving abilities over the campaign. As they take part in sessions, overcome challenges, reach goals and develop their story, characters…
regras/personagens/progressao.text:
In Astra, characters have no global levels. They grow gradually by acquiring and improving abilities over the campaign.
As they take part in sessions, overcome challenges, reach goals and develop their story, characters receive Experience Points, usually shortened to XP.
Experience Points
Experience Points represent the growth the character gains during their adventures.
XP received is added to the character's available total. When XP is spent on an improvement, its cost is removed from that total.
The character can save XP for as many sessions as they want until they have enough for the intended purchase.
Awarding XP
As a default pace, each character receives:
2 XP at the end of each session
The Narrator can use 1 XP for a slower pace or a short session, and 3 XP when the session represents a major milestone of the campaign.
It is recommended to give every character in the group the same amount of XP, keeping them at the same pace of advancement.
Spending Experience
XP can be used to:
raise Attributes;
raise Skills;
acquire or raise Competencies;
acquire or develop abilities specific to a setting or module.
Raising a trait means buying its next level. Intermediate levels cannot be skipped.
When a rule uses the term new level, use the value the trait will have after the purchase.
Example: raising a Skill from level 2 to level 3 uses 3 as the new level to calculate the cost.
When an Attribute increases, every derived value whose formula currently uses that Attribute, such as Health, Willpower, Load and Initiative, is recalculated immediately (see Derived Traits).
If a Capability replaced the Attribute of a formula, the value follows the replacement. For example, if the character's Health uses Cunning instead of Vigor, raising Cunning recalculates their Health, while raising Vigor does not change it. The replacement stays limited to the formula the Capability names.
Experience Costs
Improvement Cost 
Raise an Attribute new level × 5 XP 
Raise a Skill new level × 3 XP 
Acquire or raise a Competency new Total Competency Level × 3 XP 
Other abilities set by the rule, setting or module 
Examples
Raising an Attribute from 2 to 3 costs 15 XP.
Raising an Attribute from 3 to 4 costs 20 XP.
Acquiring the first level of a Skill costs 3 XP.
Raising a Skill from 2 to 3 costs 9 XP.
Raising a Skill from 3 to 4 costs 12 XP.
A character with Total Competency Level 2 pays 9 XP to acquire their third Competency Level.
A character with Marksman 2 pays 9 XP to raise Marksman to Level 3.
A character with Marksman 1 and another Competency at Level 1 also pays 9 XP to acquire Level 1 of a third Competency.
Acquiring and raising Competencies
The Total Competency Level is the sum of the Levels the character has in all their Competencies. This value is not a global character Level; it is used to calculate the cost of this advancement.
Acquiring or raising a Competency costs 3 × the new Total Competency Level in XP.
After paying, the character raises by 1 the Level of a Competency they already have or acquires Level 1 of a new Competency. Each increase automatically grants the content set for the new Level. No Competency can go beyond Level 5 or the maximum Level set in its progression, but there is no limit to the Total Competency Level.
Character Development
Advancement through experience lets characters who went through the same adventures develop in different ways.
One character can focus their XP on mastering a few abilities, while another can spread it across different Skills, Competencies and other options.
Spending XP represents how the experiences lived during the campaign specifically transformed the character.

criacao-de-personagem/criacao-de-persona.text:
Character Creation is the process of building a new character in Astra. The result is a sheet ready to play, with Attributes, Skills, Competencies and starting equipment.
The steps are done in order, but you can go back and adjust earlier choices while the character's concept takes shape.
Subsections
Identity — Concept, Ambition, Desire and Convictions.
Attributes and Skills — Attributes (fixed array) and Skills (profiles).
Derived Traits — Health, Willpower, Initiative and Maximum Load.
Competencies — 2 Competency Points.
Starting Equipment — what the character starts out carrying.
Finally, round out the character with a name, appearance and backstory. The sheet is ready to play; later adjustments, spending XP, follow the Advancement rules.

criacao-de-personagem/atributos-e-perici.text:
Beyond the concept, a character is defined numerically by their Attributes and Skills. This subsection covers the starting distribution of points between them.
Attributes
Every character has the six core Attributes, with values from 1 to 5 (1 = weak, 2 = average, 5 = human peak).
Distribute the fixed array below, choosing where each value goes:
One Attribute at 4 · two at 3 · two at 2 · one at 1
No Attribute can go above 4 during creation — the value 5 is only reached with XP.
Skills
Skills range from 0 to 5 (0 = untrained). Each Skill has a linked Attribute, normally used to form its Dice Pool.
The core has 24 Skills, including Acrobatics, Throwing, General Knowledge and Repair. Start with all of them at 0 and choose one of the three profiles:
Generalist — one skill at 3, six at 2 and seven at 1.
Balanced — two at 3, four at 2 and five at 1.
Specialist — one at 4, two at 3, two at 2 and two at 1.
Skills that get no points stay at 0. The cap during creation is also 4.

Some of the character's values are not chosen directly: they are calculated from the Attributes.
Trait Default formula 
Health 3 + Vigor boxes (see Health) 
Willpower 3 + Determination boxes (see Willpower) 
Initiative Pool of Cunning + Determination, rolled at the start of the Scene (see Initiative) 
Maximum Load 5 + Strength slots (see Load) 
Replacements in formulas
Capabilities and other rules can replace an Attribute used in a derived trait. The replacement affects only the given formula, does not add the two Attributes together and does not change their other roles.
For example, if a Capability says Health uses Cunning instead of Vigor, its formula becomes:
Health = 3 + Cunning
This replacement does not make Cunning work as Vigor in tests, recovery or any other rule.
When the Attribute that currently makes up a derived trait increases, the value is recalculated immediately. Capabilities always take precedence over the default formulas and over other earlier rules that set their Attributes.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/a-cena.summary: A Scene is a unit of play, whether narrative or tactical. A Tactical Scene is a Scene divided into Rounds and Turns. It starts when a conflict calls for a resolution structured in Turns and lasts until the conflict…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/a-cena.text:
A Scene is a unit of play, whether narrative or tactical.
A Tactical Scene is a Scene divided into Rounds and Turns. It starts when a conflict calls for a resolution structured in Turns and lasts until the conflict ends, whether by the defeat of one side, flight, surrender, a change in circumstances or any other outcome set by the narrative.
Within the Tactical Scene, time is divided into Rounds.
Rounds and Turns
A Round represents a full cycle of the Scene, in which every participant has the chance to act.
Within each Round, participants take their Turns in the order set by Initiative.
A Turn represents the moment when a character can act directly in the Scene.
After every participant has taken their Turn, a new Round begins, keeping the same Initiative order as long as no rule or circumstance says otherwise.
Initiative
Initiative sets the order in which participants take their Turns during the scene.
At the start of the Scene, each participant rolls a Dice Pool made of Cunning and Determination and counts Successes as usual.
Cunning + Determination = Initiative Pool
Capabilities and other rules can replace one of the Initiative Attributes or set a different Pool. When a Capability does so, it takes precedence over the default formula.
Participants act from the highest number of Successes to the lowest. If the Initiative Pool falls below 1 die, the result is 1 Success.
Ties
When a player character and an NPC tie, the player character acts first.
When two or more player characters get the same number of Successes, they can decide among themselves the order in which they act.
If they cannot agree, the Narrator sets the order.
When two or more NPCs tie, the one with the highest Cunning acts first. If the tie remains, the Narrator sets the order.
The Turn
During their Turn, a character has:
Action + Movement
The Action and the Movement can be used in whatever order the player prefers.
A character can, for example, move before taking their Action or act first and move afterward, or even move, act and move again if they still have movement points left, as explained in Movement.
How these resources are used depends on the character's decisions and the circumstances of the Scene.
Narrative vs Tactical
Not every Scene needs to be resolved at the same level of detail.
In more narrative situations, the focus is on the characters' decisions, the consequences of their actions and the development of the Scene as a whole. In those moments, there is no need to track precisely elements such as position, acting order, distances, movement or the exact duration of each action.
When those elements start to matter directly to the conflict, the Scene can take on a more tactical structure.
In a Tactical Scene, the game uses more precise rules to represent what happens moment to moment. The participants' order is set by Initiative, time is divided into Rounds and Turns, positions and distances can be tracked on a map, and each character manages resources such as their Action and their Movement.
This shift does not have to happen only in combat. Chases, escapes, infiltrations under pressure, collapses, traps or any other situation in which order, timing and positioning matter can also use a tactical structure.
Likewise, not every conflict needs to be handled this way. A quick fight, a riskless crossing or an action whose exact position does not matter can still be resolved narratively, using tests and decisions without dividing the Scene into Turns.
The purpose of this distinction is to let Astra use precision when it really adds something to the Scene, without turning every situation into a rigid sequence of actions, moves and measurements.

Using a map is recommended, with characters and other Scene elements occupying specific positions in squares.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acao.summary: An Action represents what the character can do during their Turn besides their Movement. During a Tactical Scene, the Action is the main resource used to attack, perform maneuvers, use objects, interact with the…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acao.text:
An Action represents what the character can do during their Turn besides their Movement.
During a Tactical Scene, the Action is the main resource used to attack, perform maneuvers, use objects, interact with the environment or carry out other activities relevant to the situation.
Some Actions have specific effects set by the rules. Attacking, for example, starts a Confront, while other Actions can change how the character moves or set their own procedures for resolving a given situation.
When an Action has a specific rule, that rule sets how it is resolved.
Narrative Actions
Not every Action taken during a Tactical Scene needs its own rule.
A character can try to open a door, pull a lever, take a potion from their bag and drink it, help someone, handle an object or do any other activity that fits the situation.
In these cases, the Narrator decides whether the activity can be done with a single Action and whether a test is needed to complete it.
An Action represents a meaningful activity during the Turn, not necessarily a single physical movement.
For that reason, simple actions do not need to be split into several smaller steps.
For example, drawing a potion from the bag and drinking it can count as a single Action, instead of requiring one Action to grab the item and another to use it.
Likewise, drawing a weapon before using it can be part of the Action itself when it represents a simple, continuous sequence.
This approach aims to keep the Scene's pace and avoid breaking simple activities into unnecessary steps.
During a Tactical Scene, characters should use the Basic Actions whenever one of them properly represents what they want to do.
These Actions exist to provide consistent procedures for common situations, especially those that directly affect positioning, combat and the resolution of the Scene.
A Narrative Action should be used mainly when the character's intent is not covered by any Basic Action or other specific rule of the system.
Describing an activity differently does not replace a Basic Action when, in rules terms, the character is doing the same thing.
When no existing rule properly represents the situation, the Narrator decides how the Action is resolved, including whether tests are needed or other consequences apply.
Limits
The flexibility of an Action does not mean any number of activities can be bundled freely.
The Narrator should consider the time available, the complexity of the activity and the circumstances of the Scene to decide what can be done within a single Action.
Activities that represent different goals, require lengthy procedures or have their own rules can require separate Actions.
The goal is not to measure every move the character makes, but to represent consistently what they can meaningfully accomplish during their Turn.
Basic Actions
The Basic Actions represent the most common ways to act during a Tactical Scene.
They provide standard procedures for recurring situations, such as attacking, defending, interacting with the environment or performing maneuvers. Whenever a Basic Action properly represents what the character wants to do, its rules should be used.
This helps keep the Scene's resolution consistent and prevents similar situations from being handled differently just because of how they were described.
The Basic Actions, however, do not represent everything a character can try to do. When none of them properly covers the character's intent, the action can be resolved narratively, as the Narrator decides.
List of Actions
Confront
Run
Jump
Wait
Switching Equipment
Maneuvers

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/confronta.summary: A Confront happens when a character decides to attack another character during a Tactical Scene. When starting a Confront, the attacker builds a Dice Pool according to the kind of Attack used. Kind of Attack Default…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/confronta.text:
A Confront happens when a character decides to attack another character during a Tactical Scene.
When starting a Confront, the attacker builds a Dice Pool according to the kind of Attack used.
Kind of Attack Default Pool 
Melee Agility + Fighting 
Shooting weapon Agility + Shooting 
Thrown weapon Strength + Throwing 
The weapon, a Capability or another rule can set a different Attribute or Pool. Capabilities always take precedence over other replacements.
The Heavy property replaces Agility with Strength without changing the Skill: a Heavy melee weapon uses Strength + Fighting, while a Heavy shooting weapon uses Strength + Shooting. It does not add Strength to the damage.
Two-Weapon Fighting
Every character can use one weapon in each hand by default. This lets them keep two weapons with different types and properties at hand, but by itself it grants no extra dice, damage or Attacks.
On each Confront, whether attacking or responding, the character chooses which of the two weapons to use:
the main weapon is the chosen weapon. It sets the Pool, the Damage, the Damage Type and the Special Properties of the Confront;
the off-hand weapon is the one in the other hand. It has no effect on the Confront, unless a Capability, such as those of Ambidextrous, says otherwise.
Unarmed, Natural weapons and Shields do not count as an off-hand weapon.
Responding to the Confront
After the attacker declares the Confront, the target character must choose how to respond.
They can:
Accept the Confront
Defend
Dodge
The chosen response sets how the test is resolved and which consequences can follow.
Accept the Confront
When they Accept the Confront, the character does not merely try to avoid the Attack. They respond by striking back.
Both characters build their Dice Pools and make an opposed roll.
Whoever gets more Successes wins the Confront.
If the attacker wins, they deal damage equal to:
Margin of Successes + weapon Damage
If the one who accepted the Confront wins, the counterattack deals only:
Margin of Successes, as superficial damage
The weapon's Damage does not apply to the counterattack.
The Margin is the difference between the number of Successes the two participants got.
If both get the same number of Successes, it is a tie and the attacker wins, but deals only the weapon's Damage as superficial damage.
To Accept the Confront, the responding character must be able to hit the attacker with the weapon used, observing the ranged weapon restriction (see Reach and Confront Responses).
In general, confronts between melee weapons require both to be within each other's reach, while ranged Attacks can only be answered this way when the character also has a valid way to hit the attacker.
Defend
A character equipped with a Shield can choose to Defend.
In that case, they make a roll opposed to the Attack. The Dice Pool used is:
Strength + Fighting
The Shield's Protection is added to the Dice Pool.
If the defender gets more Successes than the attacker, the Attack is blocked and neither participant deals damage.
On a tie, the attacker wins, but deals only the weapon's Damage as superficial damage.
If the attacker gets more Successes, they deal damage the same way as when winning against a target who Accepts the Confront: Margin of Successes + weapon Damage.
Defending is not a counterattack. Even when they win the roll, the character only keeps the Attack from hitting them.
Dodge
A character can choose to Dodge to try to avoid the Attack entirely.
The Dice Pool used is:
Agility + Acrobatics
Capabilities and other rules can replace this Pool. Describing the Dodge differently does not allow freely using another Attribute or Skill.
If the character gets more Successes than the attacker, they avoid the damage entirely and can immediately move up to:
half their base Movement
in a direction of their choice.
This move follows the usual Movement rules, such as Difficult Terrain and Special Movement, but does not trigger effects provoked by movement, such as abilities that punish or interfere with opponents' movement.
On a tie, the attacker wins, but deals only the weapon's Damage as superficial damage.
If the attacker gets more Successes, they deal damage the same way as when winning against a target who Accepts the Confront: Margin of Successes + weapon Damage.
A character who is unable to move cannot choose to Dodge.
Target without a Response
When the target cannot respond to the Confront, whether because they are surprised, unconscious, have no valid response or have their Dice Pool reduced below 1 die, only the attacker rolls. The target's result always counts as 1 Success.
The Confront is resolved as usual with that value, including the tie rule. If the attacker gets no Successes, the Attack fails and no one takes damage.
Numerical Advantage
When several characters surround the same enemy, the numerical advantage opens gaps in their defense.
When starting a Confront against an enemy, the attacker gets +1 die for each ally they have beyond the enemy side in that fight:
Numerical Advantage Bonus = allies adjacent to the target - (the target + the target's allies adjacent to them)
The attacker counts themselves among the allies adjacent to the target. The bonus is never negative.
Situation Bonus for each attacker 
1 × 1 +0 
2 × 1 +1 
3 × 1 +2 
3 × 2 +1 
2 × 2 +0 
To count the sides:
Adjacent includes diagonals. A creature that takes up more than one square is adjacent to everything next to any square it occupies (see Size).
The attacker must also be adjacent to the target.
Defeated characters do not count for either side.
Player characters are always allies of each other. Each NPC belongs to a side, which can be hostile, neutral or allied with the group.
Numerical Advantage applies only to melee Attacks. When the surrounded enemy attacks, the characters who respond (Accepting the Confront, Defending or Dodging) do not get the bonus.
Attacking Beyond Range
A weapon's Range is the maximum distance, in squares, at which it hits its targets without penalty.
Ranged Attacks, including thrown weapons, can hit targets beyond the weapon's normal Range. For each band of squares the size of the weapon's Range beyond its normal Range, the attacker suffers -2 dice to their Dice Pool on the Attack.
A weapon with Range 6 hits targets up to 6 squares away normally. A target between 7 and 12 squares imposes -2 dice on the Attack; between 13 and 18 squares, -4 dice; and so on.
For thrown weapons, use the throwing Range instead of the weapon's Range (see Thrown).
If the loss reduces the Dice Pool below 1 die, the Attack cannot be made.
Reach and Confront Responses
The available response depends on the characters' positions and the equipment used.
Accept the Confront requires the character to be able to hit the attacker.
Defend requires a Shield, unless a Capability allows another way, such as Parry or Cover Ally.
Dodge can be used whenever the character is able to move.
Melee weapons can start Confronts against characters using ranged weapons when they are within the necessary reach.
Likewise, characters using ranged weapons can start Confronts against melee characters, but those can only Accept the Confront if they have enough reach to hit the attacker.
Ranged weapon restriction: a character cannot Accept the Confront using a ranged weapon when the attacker uses a melee weapon, even if the attacker is within the weapon's Range. Against ranged Attacks, they can Accept as usual, as long as they can hit the attacker.

Maneuvers represent physical and tactical actions used to gain an advantage during a Tactical Scene, either by changing another character's position, condition or freedom of movement, or by preparing the character themselves to act more effectively.
Unlike a Confront, a Maneuver usually does not aim mainly to deal damage. Its purpose is to gain some advantage over the opponent, control their positioning, limit their options or improve a future action of the character themselves.
Any character can try a Maneuver.
The most common Maneuvers have their own rules, but the Narrator can also use this structure to resolve other similar actions that are not specifically described.
Performing a Maneuver
Performing a Maneuver takes an Action.
In most cases, the Maneuver is resolved through an opposed roll between the character who starts it and their target. Each Maneuver sets the Pool of whoever starts it and the Pool used to resist. Maneuvers that have no target, such as Aim, need no roll: their effect is applied as their own description says.
The Pools are fixed. Describing the Maneuver differently does not allow freely swapping its Attribute or Skill. Capabilities, equipment and other rules can set express replacements, and Capabilities always take precedence.
The Maneuver (X) property allows performing the given Maneuver up to the weapon's Reach, but does not change its Pool or grant a bonus. Heavy changes only Attacks and, for that reason, does not change a Maneuver performed with the weapon either.
If the character who started the Maneuver gets more Successes, the Maneuver's effect is applied.
On a tie, nothing happens.
Maneuvers and Capabilities
The Maneuvers presented in this section are options available to any character.
Some Capabilities can improve a Maneuver, change how it works or allow special ways to use it.
Capabilities are not needed to attempt basic Maneuvers, but they can make a character especially effective at them.

The Maneuvers described in this section do not represent every possible way to physically interfere with another character.
When a player tries something similar that is not covered by a specific Maneuver, the Narrator can treat it as a Narrative Maneuver.
In that case, the Narrator sets a Dice Pool, the way to resist and the consequences of a win, using the linked Attributes and the existing Maneuvers as a reference. Reposition
When using the Reposition Maneuver, the character uses their Action to try to move another character from their current position.
To perform the Maneuver, the character must be close enough to physically interact with the target. Usually, that means being adjacent or within the appropriate reach for the way the repositioning is done.
The Dice Pool of whoever starts it is:
Strength + Athletics
The target resists with:
Strength + Athletics

Strength + Athletics

Strength + Athletics

Strength + Athletics

Strength + Athletics

Agility + Fighting
The target resists with:
Agility + Fighting

On a tie or a win for the target, nothing happens.

Picking the weapon up from the ground takes the Switching Equipment Action, even with a free hand.

When using the Aim Maneuver, the character uses their Action to set up a ranged Attack, focusing on the target before attacking.

+2 dice to the Dice Pool of the next ranged Attack
The character can Aim over more than one Turn, building up the bonus as long as they keep their position and their focus.
The character can stack Aim a number of times equal to their Cunning. A character with Cunning 2, for example, can stack at most +4 dice.
For example, a character who Aims for two Turns builds up:
+4 dice to the Dice Pool
The accumulated bonus applies to the character's next ranged Attack, whether it uses Shooting, Throwing or another Attribute set by a rule.

Aiming neither removes nor spends the character's Movement.
They still have their Movement as usual during the Turn and can move before Aiming. However, if they move after Aiming and before making the Attack, all the time spent Aiming is wasted and the accumulated bonus is lost.
This also applies if the character is moved involuntarily.

All the accumulated bonus is lost if, before attacking, the character:
uses their Movement after Aiming;
is forcibly moved;
takes damage;
becomes Prone.
The bonus is lost as soon as the character takes damage. It also cannot be used to respond to an Attack.
When this happens, all the Actions previously used to Aim are wasted and the character must start building up the bonus again if they want to Aim once more.
Making the Attack ends the Aim, whatever the result of the roll.
Aim is tracked by the Aiming Condition: each use of Aim adds one stack.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/aguardar.summary: Acting right away is not always the best choice. When using Wait, the character gives up acting at that moment to wait for a better opportunity during the Scene. Wait can be used in two ways: Delay the Turn, waiting to…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/acoes/aguardar.text:
Acting right away is not always the best choice.
When using Wait, the character gives up acting at that moment to wait for a better opportunity during the Scene.
Wait can be used in two ways:
Delay the Turn, waiting to take the Turn later.
Ready an Action, choosing in advance what they will do if a given situation happens.
Although both represent waiting before acting, each works differently.
Delay the Turn
When they Delay the Turn, the character gives up acting in their current Initiative position and keeps waiting for a chance to rejoin the Turn order.
Delaying the Turn must be decided before any Movement or Action in the Turn.
From that moment on, the player can choose a later Turn in the Round to act.
When they decide to act, the character takes their full Turn, and the position they take at that moment becomes their new Initiative position, staying that way for the rest of the Scene.
Joining a Turn
When the character decides to stop waiting, they act immediately after the current Turn ends, whether it belongs to an ally, an opponent or an NPC. This rule applies to player characters and NPCs alike.
Current Turn → Waiting character
After that, this becomes the character's position in the Initiative order for the following Rounds.
If the character does not decide to act by the end of the Round, they automatically act last in that Round, and that becomes their new Initiative position.
Example
The starting Initiative order is:
Amara → Dorian → Guard → Iselle
On Amara's Turn, she decides to Delay the Turn.
During Dorian's Turn, Amara decides to act. Dorian finishes his Turn and Amara acts immediately after, before the Guard:
Dorian → Amara → Guard → Iselle
If Amara had instead decided to act during the Guard's Turn, the Guard would finish their Turn first and Amara would act immediately after:
Dorian → Guard → Amara → Iselle
In both cases, this becomes Amara's new Initiative position for the rest of the Scene.
Ready an Action
When they Ready an Action, the character uses their Action on their own Turn to set in advance something they will do if a given situation happens.
To do so, the player must declare:
which Action will be taken;
which condition will trigger that Action.
For example:
"If the guard comes through the door, I start a Confront against them."
"If anyone gets close to the lever, I run to it."
The condition must be clear and represent something that can be objectively identified during the Scene.
When the Action happens
When the declared condition happens, the character can immediately take the Action they readied.
The condition happens first and, as soon as it is met, the readied Action is taken before the character who triggered the condition carries on with other activities in their Turn.
For example, if the condition is:
"When the guard enters the room, I attack."
The guard first enters the room, meeting the condition. Before they carry on with their Turn, the readied Action is taken.
Once it is resolved, the interrupted Turn continues as usual, if still possible.
Action set in advance
The Action taken must be the one declared when it was readied.
The player can decide not to take the Action when its condition happens, but cannot swap it at that moment for a different Action.
If they want to do something else, they must wait for their next Turn as usual.
Action requirements
When the condition happens, the character still needs to be able to take the readied Action.
All the usual requirements still apply, including reach, equipment, position and any other limitations.
For example, readying a Confront against someone does not allow taking it if the target is out of reach when the condition happens.
If the readied Action involves moving, the character uses the Movement they did not spend on their Turn. If the readied Action is Run, the extra squares are added to that remaining Movement.
Duration
A readied Action stays available until the start of the character's next Turn.
If the condition does not happen before then, the readied Action is lost.
On the new Turn, the character can act normally or use their Action again to ready another.
Initiative
Unlike Delay the Turn, Readying an Action does not change the character's Initiative position.
The character keeps their usual position in the following Rounds, no matter when their readied Action is taken.
Example
The Initiative order is:
Amara → Guard → Dorian
During her Turn, Amara declares:
"I ready a Confront. If the Guard comes through the door, I attack them."
Amara uses her Action to ready this response.
On the Guard's Turn, they move and come through the door. Amara's condition is met.
Before the Guard carries on with their Turn, Amara takes the readied Confront.
Once the Confront is resolved, the Guard carries on with their Turn as usual, if they still can.
In the following Round, Amara keeps her original Initiative position.

regras/cenas-e-conflitos/zonas.summary: A Zone represents an effect that occupies an area and affects the creatures inside it. The rule or Capability that creates a Zone sets its shape, size, range, position, duration, effects and, when applicable, its Damage…
regras/cenas-e-conflitos/zonas.text:
A Zone represents an effect that occupies an area and affects the creatures inside it.
The rule or Capability that creates a Zone sets its shape, size, range, position, duration, effects and, when applicable, its Damage and Damage Type.
By default, a Zone affects every creature inside it, including the allies of whoever created it. A creature whose space takes up more than one square is affected only once by the same Zone.
Damage Zones
When a creature is hit by a damage Zone, it makes a test of:
Agility + Acrobatics
The rule or Capability that created the Zone can set a different Dice Pool.
Each Success on the test is applied as follows:
while there is aggravated damage, the Success converts 1 point of that damage to superficial;
once all the damage has been converted, each remaining Success removes 1 point of superficial damage.
Example
A creature is hit by a Damage 4 Zone.
Successes Damage taken 
0 4 aggravated 
2 2 aggravated and 2 superficial 
4 4 superficial 
5 3 superficial 
8 or more no damage 
Interactions
A Zone is neither an Attack nor a Confront. The Accept the Confront, Defend and Dodge Responses are not used.
Resisting a Zone is not Dodging. Bonuses, penalties and replacements specific to Dodge do not apply, unless a rule says otherwise.
Resisting a Zone does not move the creature.
Base Absorption and the Absorption granted by armor do not apply to a Zone's damage.
Resistances to the Zone's Damage Type and Material, if any, convert aggravated damage to superficial as with any damage: each point of Resistance converts 1 point of the Zone's aggravated damage to superficial before the test's Successes are applied.
Vulnerabilities to the Zone's Damage Type and Material, if any, directly increase its Damage.
Immunity to the Zone's Damage Type or Material prevents the damage entirely.
Duration
A Zone can be instant or persistent.
Instant: resolves its effect as soon as it is created and then disappears.
Persistent: stays in place for the duration set by the rule or Capability that created it. That source also sets when the Zone affects a creature, such as on entering it or starting the Turn inside it.

regras/competencias/competencias.text:
Competencies represent developed ways of acting, fighting, thinking or interacting with the world. Each has its own identity and a fixed progression.
A character can develop several Competencies and combine their progressions freely.
Level
Every Competency has a Level from 0 to 5, unless its progression sets a lower maximum Level.
Level 0: the character does not have the Competency;
Levels 1 to 5: the character has every Capability granted up to that Level.
Simpler Competencies can have fewer Levels. In that case, the last Level in its progression table is its maximum Level.
Each increase automatically grants the content set for the new Level. There are no choices from a catalog and no separate purchase for the Capability.
To reach a Level, the character must have every previous Level of the same Competency. No Competency can go beyond Level 5 or the maximum Level set in its progression.
Capabilities
Capabilities are the mechanical effects granted by a Competency's Levels. They can change any part of the system when their description says so, including Pools, Successes, Actions, Maneuvers, damage, movement, range, resources, traits and formulas.
A Capability can also replace an Attribute, a Skill or another rule. When there is a conflict, the Capability's more specific rule takes precedence within the context it describes.
Choices can be part of how a Capability works, but they do not change the Competency's fixed progression.
More than one Competency
The character can have Levels in several Competencies.
Focusing Levels on a single Competency rewards specialization and brings the character closer to its Level 5. Spreading Levels across Competencies broadens their versatility and lets them combine different styles.
Total Competency Level
The Total Competency Level is the sum of the Levels the character has in all their Competencies.
Total Competency Level = sum of the Levels of every Competency.
This value is not a global character Level. It exists to set the cost of acquiring new Competency Levels.
Character creation
During character creation, each character receives 2 Competency Points.
Each point raises a Competency by 1 Level and automatically grants that Level's content. The points can be used to start with:
Level 2 in one Competency; or
Level 1 in two different Competencies.
Unused Competency Points are not converted into XP.
Acquiring during the campaign
To acquire any new Competency Level, the character pays a cost based on the new Total Competency Level:
XP cost = new Total Competency Level × 3.
After paying, the character raises by 1 the Level of a Competency they already have or acquires Level 1 of a new Competency. The new Level's content is received automatically and needs no further XP.
Current Total Level New Total Level Cost 
2 3 9 XP 
3 4 12 XP 
4 5 15 XP 
5 6 18 XP 
6 7 21 XP 
There is no limit to the Total Competency Level. The steadily rising XP cost naturally limits how many Levels are accumulated.
Format of a Competency
Each Competency presents:
its name and a description of its identity;
its Level progression;
the name and mechanical effect of its Capabilities and what each Level grants.
A Level can grant a new Capability, more than one effect of the same advance, or increase the potency of a Capability the character already has.
List of Competencies
Acrobat — Dodges that carry you farther, greater Movement, resisting being surrounded and escaping Zones.
Ambidextrous — fighting with a weapon in each hand, adding the off-hand weapon's Damage as dice when Attacking, Dodging and Parrying.
Parrier — Parrying Attacks with your own weapon, adding its Damage when Defending, first in melee and then at range as well.
Assassin — acting first in Initiative, extra damage against targets without a response and Stealth outside combat.
Marksman — preparation, keeping the Aim, precision and ranged shots with the Shooting Skill.
Hunter — tracking with Survival, studying any non-Humanoid creature with Nature or Occultism and stronger strikes against Read prey.
Captivating — beauty and presence that favor social interactions and make a stronger first impression.
Duelist — fighting with a weapon in one hand and the other free, facing isolated targets and challenging opponents.
Furious — Fury, melee aggression and damage that grows with the wounds suffered.
Guardian — Defending with a Shield for yourself and your allies: Cover Ally on Defend and Dodge, swapping places to take an Attack, Protection against Zones and blocking on a tie.
Inspirer — Helping allies at range, strengthening the Help bonus and recovering Willpower.
Mentalist — reading people and enemies through the Read Condition, Cunning on Attacks and social tests.
Robust — a larger Health track that grows with the Competency's Level.
Sentinel — Opportunity Attacks against anyone who leaves your melee weapon's reach or attacks your allies, stopping the target's movement.

regras/competencias/acrobata.title: Acrobat
regras/competencias/acrobata.summary: Acrobat represents the character who slips past blows, crosses the battlefield and refuses to be surrounded.
regras/competencias/acrobata.text:
Acrobat represents the character who slips past blows, crosses the battlefield and refuses to be surrounded.
Progression
Level Capability granted Light Feet 
1 Acrobatic Dodge — 
2 Light Feet +2 
3 Hard to Surround +3 
4 Evasion +4 
5 Untouchable +5 
Level 1 — Acrobatic Dodge
When you win a Dodge, you can move up to your full base Movement, instead of half of it.
During this movement, you can pass through squares occupied by enemies, but you cannot end it in one of them.
Level 2 — Light Feet
Your base Movement increases by a number of squares equal to your Acrobat Level. The increase also applies to Run and to the movement when Dodging.
In addition:
Difficult Terrain costs only 1 Movement point per square for you. Special Movement still costs 2 points;
standing up from Prone costs only 1 Movement point. With Movement 0, you still cannot stand up.
Level 3 — Hard to Surround
Attackers do not get Numerical Advantage against you. You still count as usual toward your allies' Numerical Advantage.
During your Movement, you can pass through squares occupied by enemies. Each one costs 1 extra Movement point, and you cannot end your movement in one of them.
These effects do not work while you are unable to move.
Level 4 — Evasion
When resisting a Damage Zone, if you get Successes equal to or greater than the Zone's Damage and can leave the area with the movement of a won Dodge, you move out of the Zone and take no damage. The movement must end outside the Zone's area.
If you do not get enough Successes, cannot leave the area or choose not to move, resisting the Zone is resolved as usual.
Level 5 — Untouchable
When Dodging, you win on a tie: you avoid all damage and can make the Acrobatic Dodge movement.

regras/competencias/ambidestro.summary: Ambidextrous represents the fighter who uses both weapons in the same strike: while one opens the enemy's guard, the other lands the blow. The Capabilities of this Competency require a melee weapon held in each hand…
regras/competencias/ambidestro.text:
Ambidextrous represents the fighter who uses both weapons in the same strike: while one opens the enemy's guard, the other lands the blow.
The Capabilities of this Competency require a melee weapon held in each hand, following Two-Weapon Fighting. The off-hand weapon must have the Light Property and be able to reach the target.
Progression
Level Capability granted 
1 Double Strike 
2 Cross Guard 
3 Ambidexterity 
Level 1 — Double Strike
When you start a Confront with a melee Attack or Accept the Confront with a melee weapon, you add to the Pool a number of dice equal to the off-hand weapon's Damage:
Pool = the main weapon's Attack Pool + off-hand weapon Damage
The damage dealt is still the main weapon's.
Level 2 — Cross Guard
When you Dodge or Parry a melee Attack, you also add the off-hand weapon's Damage to the Pool as dice.
When Parrying, the main weapon is the one used to Parry and adds its own Damage normally.
Level 3 — Ambidexterity
The off-hand weapon can be any one-handed melee weapon, not only a Light weapon.

regras/competencias/aparador.title: Parrier
regras/competencias/aparador.summary: Parrier represents the character trained to block blows with their own weapon, without relying on a shield.
regras/competencias/aparador.text:
Parrier represents the character trained to block blows with their own weapon, without relying on a shield.
Progression
Level Capability granted 
1 Parry 
2 Parry Projectiles 
Level 1 — Parry
You can choose to Defend against a melee Attack using a melee weapon you are holding, even without a Shield.
When Parrying, instead of the normal Defend Pool, you use the same Pool as a melee Attack with the weapon used and, in place of the Shield's Protection, add the weapon's Damage:
Parry Pool = the weapon's Attack Pool + weapon Damage
Rules that change the weapon's Attack Pool, such as Heavy or a Capability, also apply to Parrying.
Bonuses and penalties that depend on starting an Attack, such as Numerical Advantage, do not apply to Parrying.
The Damage counted includes the +1 of a Flexible weapon held in both hands. The weapon's Special Properties are not triggered when Parrying. The rest follows the normal Defend rules.
If you are fighting with two weapons, you choose which of them you use to Parry. The Damage of the two weapons is not added together, except through the Ambidextrous Cross Guard.
If you are also equipped with a Shield, you choose when Defending whether to use the Shield's Protection or the weapon's Damage. The two bonuses do not stack.
Unarmed and other Natural weapons cannot be used to Parry, unless another Capability allows it.
Level 2 — Parry Projectiles
You can also Parry ranged Attacks, including shots and thrown weapons, still using a melee weapon.

regras/competencias/assassino.title: Assassin
regras/competencias/assassino.summary: Assassin represents the character who reaches the target unnoticed, acts first and strikes before the opponent can react.
regras/competencias/assassino.text:
Assassin represents the character who reaches the target unnoticed, acts first and strikes before the opponent can react.
Progression
Level Capability granted Sneak Attack Silent Steps 
1 First Strike — — 
2 Sneak Attack +2 — 
3 Silent Steps +3 +3 dice 
4 Lethal Approach +4 +4 dice 
5 — +5 +5 dice 
Level 1 — First Strike
Your Initiative Pool can use Agility instead of Determination:
Initiative Pool = Cunning + Agility
If the Tactical Scene begins without the enemies having noticed your presence, you also add to your Initiative Pool a number of dice equal to your Stealth Level. The Narrator decides whether the enemies had already noticed you.
When you start a Confront against a target whose first Turn in the Scene has not yet come, the target is considered surprised and becomes a target without a response.
A target who used Delay the Turn is not considered surprised. A participant who joins the Scene after it begins is considered surprised until their first Turn comes.
Level 2 — Sneak Attack
When you win an Attack against a target without a response, you add to the damage an amount equal to your Assassin Level.
The bonus applies whatever the reason the target cannot respond: surprised by First Strike, unconscious, Paralyzed or with their Pool reduced below 1 die. It also applies outside a Tactical Scene, when the Narrator determines that the target does not notice the Attack.
The bonus adds to the weapon's Damage, applies to any kind of Attack and does not add dice to the Pool. It does not apply on a tie.
Level 3 — Silent Steps
You get a number of extra dice equal to your Assassin Level on every Stealth and Sleight of Hand test.
This bonus does not apply to the Initiative Pool, nor to the Stealth Level added by First Strike.
Level 4 — Lethal Approach
On your first Turn of each Tactical Scene, you get the effect of the Run Action without spending your Action.
